The GEO method, part 1: make your firm readable by AI engines The GEO method, part 2: give AI engines a reason to cite you How to measure your AI visibility GEO for law firms: what it looks like in practice What generative engine optimization services should include Key takeaways Frequently asked questions Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the practice of shaping your content, your website, and your presence across the web so that AI engines such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, and AI Mode cite or recommend you in their answers. SEO earns a place in a list of links; GEO earns a place inside the answer itself. For a law firm, the stakes are concrete. A prospective client who asks ChatGPT "who handles wrongful termination cases in Chicago?" gets a written answer that names two or three firms, often without clicking anything. If your firm is not one of them, it was never considered. Google is moving the same way: in our October 2026 analysis of 91 US search results pages on law firm marketing topics, 88 displayed an AI Overview. This guide defines GEO, summarizes the research behind it, compares it with SEO and answer engine optimization (AEO), and lays out the six-step method we use with law firms. What is generative engine optimization? A generative engine is a search tool that writes its answer instead of returning ten blue links. It runs one or several searches, reads the pages it retrieves, and synthesizes a response with a large language model. Sources appear as numbered citations, as link cards, or sometimes only as paraphrased facts with no visible credit. A definition you can use Generative engine optimization is the set of techniques that make your content more likely to be retrieved, trusted, and cited by AI engines when they build an answer. The goal is not a ranking position but a share of the answer: being quoted, paraphrased, or recommended by name in the response the user actually reads. Where the term comes from The term was coined in a research paper, "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" , by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues from Princeton University, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI, and IIT Delhi. It was first posted on arXiv in November 2023 and presented at KDD 2024, a major data science conference. The paper treats AI engines as a black box and asks a simple question: what changes to a web page make an engine use it more? What GEO covers in practice Three conditions decide whether a model uses your page. Retrieval : the engine must be able to crawl your page and find it when it searches. Trust : the page must come from a source the engine can identify and verify, such as a named attorney at a real firm. Extractability : the page must state facts clearly enough that a model can lift them into an answer without guessing. That is why we treat GEO as an extension of law firm SEO , not a replacement. Retrieval still runs largely on search indexes, so the SEO groundwork stays. GEO adds the work on trust and extractability that classic rankings never fully rewarded. What the GEO research actually tested Most GEO advice you will read traces back to this paper, so it is worth knowing what it found, and what it did not. The setup: 10,000 queries and nine tactics The researchers built GEO-bench, a benchmark of 10,000 queries drawn from nine sources and spread across 25 domains. They rewrote source pages using nine methods: authoritative tone, statistics addition, keyword stuffing, citing sources, quotation addition, easy-to-understand wording, fluency optimization, unique words, and technical terms. Then they measured how much of each answer drew on the rewritten page, weighted by position, plus a subjective impression score. The three tactics that won: citations, quotations, statistics Three methods stood out. Citing credible sources, adding quotations from relevant sources, and replacing vague statements with statistics produced a relative improvement of 30 to 40% on the position-adjusted word count metric and 15 to 30% on subjective impression. The abstract sums it up: GEO "can boost visibility by up to 40% in generative engine responses." One finding matters directly to lawyers. The paper reports that the "Law & Government" domain benefits significantly from statistics addition. Data-backed legal content, such as deadlines, filing thresholds, or court statistics with their source, is the kind of content the models favored in these tests. Edits for fluency and readability also helped, by 15 to 30%. What failed, and who gains the most Keyword stuffing, the oldest SEO trick, offered little to no improvement. In a live test on Perplexity, it performed 10% worse than the unmodified page, while quotation addition improved visibility by 22% and statistics addition by up to 37%. The most encouraging result concerns smaller players. Pages ranked fifth in the classic search results gained 115.1% in visibility with the cite sources method, while the same method cut the visibility of first-ranked pages by 30.3% on average. A solo practitioner or small law firm with well-sourced pages can win a place in the answer against bigger names. Keep the limits in mind: the tests ran in 2023 and 2024, on a research engine and on Perplexity, and the engines have changed since. Treat the numbers as a direction, not a guarantee. GEO vs SEO vs AEO: is GEO better than SEO? GEO is not better than SEO, because it depends on it. The three disciplines target different surfaces of the same search journey, and a law firm needs all three working together. Three disciplines, three goals Criterion SEO AEO GEO Goal Rank in the list of results Be the direct answer to a question Be cited or recommended inside an AI-generated answer Main surfaces Google and Bing organic results, local pack Featured snippets, People Also Ask, voice assistants ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, Gemini, Copilot Key signals Relevance, backlinks, technical quality A concise answer to a well-defined question Retrievability, verifiable facts, cited sources, entity clarity Content format Pages built around a target keyword Question followed by a short answer Answer-first sections with sourced data and named authors Main KPI Rankings, clicks, consultations Snippet ownership Citation share, brand mentions, AI referrals Answer engine optimization came first, with featured snippets and voice assistants: write one clear answer to one question. GEO keeps that habit and adds what generative engines need before they trust you: sources, data, and an author they can identify across the web. Where the strategies diverge In SEO, you optimize to be found. In GEO, you optimize to be understood and reused. That means fewer generic pages and more pages that answer one precise question, with a named attorney, a visible update date, and facts a model can quote word for word. Rankings and citations do not always match. A competitor with an average website can be cited regularly if its pages are precise and attributable, and a firm that ranks well can be left out of the AI answer. That gap is the opportunity for firms that move early. Is SEO dead now with AI? No. Google's documentation says there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode: a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet, the same rules as classic search. If your pages are not indexed, most engines will never retrieve them. Google even says that clicks from results pages with AI Overviews are "higher quality," meaning visitors spend more time on the site. How do AI engines choose their sources? Every engine follows the same broad pattern: rewrite the question into searches, retrieve candidate pages, then let a language model pick the passages that best support an answer. The details differ by engine, and they explain most GEO tactics. ChatGPT search According to OpenAI's help center, ChatGPT search "sometimes partners with other search providers," Microsoft among them, and rewrites your question into one or more targeted queries, adding an approximate location for local searches. Its own crawler, OAI-SearchBot, collects pages for search answers, and OpenAI states that sites opted out of it will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers. Our guide on how to get cited by ChatGPT covers the tactics specific to it. Perplexity Perplexity searches the web as it answers and shows numbered citations that link to each source. Its crawler, PerplexityBot, is "designed to surface and link websites in search results on Perplexity," and the company says it is not used to train AI foundation models. Because every source is visible, Perplexity is the easiest engine to audit. More in our guide to Perplexity for lawyers . Google AI Overviews and AI Mode Google's AI features draw on its regular search index and use a "query fan-out" technique: they issue multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources to build one answer. That is why a page that answers a narrow sub-question well can be cited for a broad query. Google adds that no AI text file or special schema markup is required. See our guides to AI Overviews for law firms and Google AI Mode . Across engines, a source gets cited when the engine can retrieve it, confirm who wrote it, and find a passage that answers the exact question on its own. The GEO method, part 1: make your firm readable by AI engines Our method has six steps in two blocks. The first block is technical: it makes sure AI engines can reach, read, and identify your firm. Without it, the content work in part 2 goes unseen. Step 1. Set your robots directives for AI crawlers Many law firm websites block AI bots without knowing it, through a security plugin, a CDN setting, or a copied robots.txt file. Each AI company runs separate bots for search and for model training, and you can treat them differently. The table below summarizes what each one does, according to each company's own documentation. Bot Company What it does Our default OAI-SearchBot OpenAI Finds pages for ChatGPT search answers Allow ChatGPT-User OpenAI Visits a page when a user asks ChatGPT to Allow GPTBot OpenAI Collects content to train OpenAI's models Firm's choice PerplexityBot Perplexity Indexes pages for Perplexity answers, not used for training Allow Claude-SearchBot Anthropic Improves the quality of Claude's search results Allow ClaudeBot Anthropic Collects content that may be used to train Claude Firm's choice Google-Extended Google Controls use of your content for Gemini training and grounding, with no effect on Google Search Firm's choice Blocking a training bot does not remove you from the matching search product: OpenAI's documentation states that each setting is independent, so you can allow OAI-SearchBot while disallowing GPTBot. Blocking a search bot, on the other hand, can take you out of that engine's answers. Allowing training bots may help models learn your firm's name over time; blocking them is a legitimate choice if you object to your content being reused. Check your CDN and firewall too, since Google's guidance names hosting infrastructure as a place where crawling gets blocked. The Perplexity and Anthropic help pages give the exact user agents, also listed in our glossary entry on AI crawlers . Step 2. Describe your firm and attorneys with structured data Structured data will not get you into an AI answer by itself; Google says no special schema is needed. Its value is clarity: it tells engines that the Jane Doe on your bio page is the same attorney as the Jane Doe in the state bar directory. Use LegalService for the firm (schema.org now marks the older Attorney type as deprecated), Person for each lawyer, and Article for guides, with author and update dates. The key property is sameAs . On each Person, list the URLs of that attorney's state bar profile, Avvo, Justia, LinkedIn, and any other directory listing. Keep the markup consistent with what the page visibly says, which Google lists among its best practices for AI features. Step 3. Add an llms.txt file, without expecting miracles An llms.txt file is a short Markdown file at the root of your site that gives AI agents a curated map of your most useful pages. Jeremy Howard published the proposal in September 2024. It is cheap to create and harmless. But Google states plainly that you don't need "AI text files" to appear in its AI features, so treat llms.txt as a convenience for agents that read it, not as a way to get cited. The GEO method, part 2: give AI engines a reason to cite you Once engines can read you, these three steps decide whether they choose you. Step 4. Write answer-first pages that stand on their own Models extract passages, not whole pages. Each section should answer one question in its first sentence, then explain. If a prospective client asks how long they have to sue after a car accident in Texas, your page should open with: "In Texas, you generally have two years from the date of the injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 16.003)." The details and exceptions come after. Apply this to every practice area page and guide: one page per question, a direct answer under each H2, short paragraphs, and tables for comparisons. Add a visible "last updated" date. Bing's guidance on AI answers stresses that regular updates help AI systems reference the most current version of your content, and legal answers age fast. Step 5. Back every claim with citations, quotations, and statistics This is the step the GEO paper measured directly. Turn vague statements into sourced facts: cite the statute, the court rule, or the agency page; quote the exact text of the law or a court's holding; replace "many cases settle" with a number and its source. These edits take little time, and they match the three tactics that raised visibility by 30 to 40% in the research. Legal ethics still apply to anything an engine might quote. Under ABA Model Rule 7.1, no communication about your services may be false or misleading, and Rule 7.2(c) limits who can claim to be a certified specialist. Present past results with context, and check your state bar's rules, as covered in our guide to lawyer advertising rules . Step 6. Build your entity across the web Engines trust what they can confirm in several independent places. For a US lawyer, the core profiles are the state bar's public attorney directory, Avvo, Justia, Martindale-Hubbell, FindLaw, Super Lawyers if you are selected, LinkedIn , and your Google Business Profile. Directories such as Avvo often list attorneys before they ever sign up, so you may already have a profile waiting to be claimed. Then make the details match everywhere: firm name, attorney names, address and phone number ( NAP ), bar admissions, and practice areas, the groundwork of local SEO for law firms . Each attorney needs a real author page on your site with bar admissions, education, and links to those profiles, and every article should carry a byline that points to it. These are the E-E-A-T signals Google describes, and they show AI engines who stands behind the content. Earned mentions complete the picture: a quote in a local newspaper, an article in a bar journal, a podcast interview, a CLE presentation. Run your target questions in Perplexity, note which third-party sites it cites for your practice area, and aim for a presence on at least one of them each quarter. The goal is not an exact score but a trend, and a list of blind spots to fix. Build a prompt panel and test it monthly List 10 to 20 questions your prospective clients actually ask, mixing informational questions ("how is child support calculated in Ohio?") with hiring questions ("best DUI lawyer in Phoenix"). Run them every month in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode, and Gemini, from a logged-out browser in your city. Record whether your firm is named, which page is cited, and which competitors appear instead. Use the free data the platforms already give you Google includes AI Overviews and AI Mode traffic in the overall Web search data of the Search Console Performance report. Bing goes further. Since February 2026, Bing Webmaster Tools has offered an AI Performance report , in public preview, showing how often your pages are cited in Microsoft Copilot and Bing's AI summaries, which URLs are cited, and the grounding queries behind them. Microsoft calls it an early step toward GEO tooling. In GA4, set up an exploration or a custom channel for referrals from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com, and copilot.microsoft.com. Part of this traffic arrives without a referrer and is counted as direct, so treat the figure as a floor. What matters for a law firm is whether these visits turn into calls and consultation requests. What is the best tool for generative engine optimization? No single tool sees inside every engine. For tracking at scale, Ahrefs Brand Radar monitors brand mentions and cited pages across AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Copilot, and the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit tracks how brands appear in AI answers, including ChatGPT and Google AI Mode. For most small firms, a monthly prompt panel plus Bing's free report gives enough signal to act. A minimal GEO tracking protocol in four steps 1. Write 10 to 20 prospective-client questions, with your city where relevant. 2. Test them monthly in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode, and Gemini, and log which firms and pages are cited. 3. Check the Bing Webmaster Tools AI Performance report and your GA4 AI referrals each month. 4. List the three third-party sites cited most often in your practice area and earn a presence on one of them this quarter. GEO for law firms: what it looks like in practice Small and midsize firms are well placed to benefit. National directories dominate classic rankings through sheer volume, but a precise, well-documented firm rooted in one city can earn its place in AI answers on high-value questions. A worked example A business owner asks Perplexity: "Which lawyer in Austin can help me sell my small business?" The answer cites two or three sources. A firm with a dedicated page on selling a business, a byline from a named attorney admitted in Texas, matching Avvo and state bar profiles, and a mention in a local business journal has a real chance of being cited. A firm with none of those signals will not be, however well it ranks. Matching AI queries with content Type of AI query GEO-optimized content Expected result "Best employment lawyer in Chicago for wrongful termination" Wrongful termination page, attorney bio with Illinois bar admission, complete Google Business Profile Firm named in local hiring answers "How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Texas?" Answer-first guide citing the statute, with exceptions and an update date Page cited as the source in informational answers "Do I need a lawyer for an uncontested divorce in Florida?" Direct answer, sourced costs and timelines, named Florida attorney Cited in AI Overviews and Perplexity for the question and its variants The payoff is the ratio of effort to visibility. Five strong, well-sourced pages on your core practice areas, backed by a consistent entity across the web, keep working long after a paid campaign stops. That is what we see at Hendy with the firms that built these signals early. What generative engine optimization services should include If you hire an agency for GEO, judge the offer on method and measurement, not on buzzwords. A serious engagement covers both the technical side and the editorial side. The deliverables to expect A crawl audit of robots.txt, CDN, and firewall rules for AI bots. Structured data for the firm and each attorney, with sameAs links. A rewrite plan for priority pages: answer-first sections, citations, statistics. An entity cleanup: consistent NAP, claimed profiles, author pages. A prompt panel and monthly reporting on citations, mentions, and AI referral leads. Red flags Be wary of anyone who guarantees citations in ChatGPT or a spot in AI Overviews: no one controls these answers, just as no one can guarantee the top position on Google. Be equally wary of mass-produced AI content and of offers that sell GEO apart from SEO. The two share the same foundation, which is why our law firm SEO services handle both together. Key takeaways AI engines do not simply cite the pages that rank best on Google. They cite the sources they can retrieve, identify, and quote with confidence. For a law firm, generative engine optimization comes down to six steps: open access to AI search crawlers, add structured data, publish llms.txt as a small extra, write answer-first pages, source every claim, and keep your entity consistent across the web. Then measure every month. Firms that start now take a lead that is hard to close, because the pages, profiles, and mentions behind a citation take months to build. Google's AI features draw on its search index, and ChatGPT search relies in part on third-party search providers, so a page that is not indexed or ranked is rarely retrieved. text: Digital marketing is one of those exciting-yet-frustrating fields in which any technique you master is virtually guaranteed to need an update as soon as you have gotten comfortable with it. The upside for those of us working in the industry is that we never have a chance to get bored! The challenge for our clients is that, no matter how recently we have answered a question about the “best” way to get views and clicks online, we are probably going to find ourselves answering again almost before we have a chance to catch our breath. For the past several months, many of the most pressing questions I have been hearing from clients have come from GEO: What is it, should I be worried about it, how can I make sure my law firm is actually visible in all these AI answers? Here’s what your law firm needs to know to stay relevant as the search landscape evolves. What Is GEO, Anyway? Sponsored Content, Legal Technology Modernizing Legal Workflows: A More Connected Lexis+® With Protégé™ Experience Legal work rarely happens one task at a time. Research leads to drafting. Drafting surfaces new research questions. Reviewing a document can send a legal professional back to the underlying authority. By LexisNexis GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization, and the term is one of several competing names for the set of techniques that, depending on whom you ask, may be thought of as a successor to SEO (search engine optimization) or its natural continuation. GEO builds on many of the same principles as SEO, but adapts their implementation to account for differences in the ways “answer engines” leverage generative AI access and present information when compared to the familiar operations of established search engines (e.g., Google). How Do AI Search Tools Source Information? The first thing you probably need to know, if you are developing a law firm GEO strategy, is that AI search tools (at least for now) overwhelmingly source their information from “traditional” search engines. The dominant player in the search engine space is still Google, but ChatGPT has been known to prioritize results from Bing . Even accounting for the differences between the various search engines currently managing a share of total search traffic, these tools operate on essentially similar principles. This means they also tend to use closely related criteria for evaluating topical relevance when determining which sources to return in response to a query. Learn how Managing Attorney oversight turns AI-driven review into a more adaptive, strategic and defensible process. By Trustpoint.One People sometimes lose sight of one of the “big picture” implications of the information-sourcing behavior used by answer engines. If the AI search tools are getting the information they compile and synthesize to provide their users with concise answers to direct questions (rather than lists of relevant links for the users to review on their own) by running searches themselves, then SEO cannot logically go anywhere if you want your law firm website to show up in those answers. It doesn’t matter whether the search is initiated by a human being or a large language model (LLM): If your page is not in the search results, nobody will be seeing it, much less visiting it. Multi-Query Search That does not mean that there are no differences between an AI tool’s search behavior and what you or I would do if we sat down to enter a Google query. The exact protocols tend to be closely guarded secrets, but one common theme across all of the generative engine search tools currently in widespread consumer use is that they use a technique similar to what Google calls the “query fan-out” method. You can find several detailed explanations of how query fan-out works online, but for the sake of simplifying a complex topic with a lot of caveats, let’s just say that the way LLMs handle requests for search-based answers is that they take the question the user has asked, and then they generate a set of additional questions that are intended to be subsidiary to the original query. When the method works well, these sub-queries are one or both of the following: Questions the user would need the answers to in order to understand the answer to their original query Questions from whose answers a reasonable person could infer the answer to the original query Some tools, like Perplexity, will be so obliging as to show the sub-queries generated in order to locate the information they will use to answer the original user query. Implications for Law Firm GEO Strategy At this point, we can begin to draw some inferences of our own. Let’s walk them out together. #1. Content Pillars Are More Important Than Ever If you are familiar with the structure and function of content pillars, you know that these treasure troves of content work by creating a large set of interrelated articles/pages, each rich in keywords, and cross-linking them. Usually you will find that pillars follow something of a pyramidal structure: A very long central “pillar” that aims to provide comprehensive coverage of a topic, 3-4 somewhat shorter pages covering different aspects of that topic in greater detail, and then 3-4 smaller articles for each of these “subtopic” pages. This structure is absolutely phenomenal for creating the sub-query relevance that helps to place a page within a generative answer engine’s list of reviewed sources. #2. Keyword Gap Strategy Still Works Traditional content pillars are often based on the concept of “keyword gap” coverage. Keyword gap analysis is a mainstay of SEO strategy that works by identifying keywords for which your competitors are ranking well in search results, but your site is not. One of the main functions of content pillars is to “plug” the keyword gap, to make sure that your website is effectively covering high-value keywords for which your competitors are consistently out-performing you. The kind of coverage this exercise creates lends itself naturally to a spread that captures a wide range of possible subqueries for the pillar’s “core” keyword. A content pillar is usually a single, massive project (that may sometimes get updates, as needed), so to build on the foundation it establishes many SEOs will also use keyword gap analysis in establishing a set of content “buckets” that will be used to define topics you want to target going forward. This same technique can be deployed very effectively in modern GEO: Adjust your “buckets” to align with questions and their likely subqueries related to your practice area(s). #3. Comprehensiveness Is Key The bad news, for law firms seeking to upgrade their GEO strategy, is that the subquery generation technique used by LLMs, in all their multiple variations, strongly privileges comprehensive topical coverage. If you want your individual pages to stay “on-topic” (a key factor in demonstrating page relevance for the search engines on whose results the answer tools will be drawing), then the need to cover any topic you want to “rank” for (”list” might be a better word than “rank” when it comes to GEO) will likely mean that you need to increase the number of individual pieces of content on your law firm website, and in some cases the rate at which you are adding to your website content (the current frequency of your website updates will obviously matter here). The good news, if you are worried about how to adapt your law firm content marketing strategy for the new era of GEO, is that almost any legal topic can be covered from many different angles. The fact that LLM-based answer engines will be examining several of them every time they review sources to generate an answer in response to a user’s request means that these AI search tools actually give your law firm more, not fewer, chances to be recognized as relevant and therefore show up in the results eventually displayed to users. To take advantage of the multiplying opportunities, what you will want to do is work with a digital marketing professional (or agency) who can help you round out a truly comprehensive GEO content creation strategy that starts with the keyword “classics” familiar from SEO and builds outward to answer an ever wider set of thematically-related questions. Take GEO as an Opportunity, Not Just a Challenge Generative answer engines’ use of traditional search engines to source information in response to user requests will continue to keep SEO relevant, even as the digital marketing industry continues to evolve alongside customers’ behavior. If your law firm has an effective SEO strategy already: Build on it! If your law firm’s SEO game has been weak, now is the time to address the underlying issues that are keeping your site from ranking. In either case, rather than moving away from SEO toward GEO you will want to look at ways to enhance your total content strategy based on the way answer engines select their sources and present their responses. Work with an experienced digital marketing specialist to identify high-value topics and subqueries in your practice area, and start working to build your comprehensive suite of answers to the real questions people really ask about the type of cases your firm handles. text: Insight GEO for Law Firms: What It Is and How to Optimize for AI Search A seven-step audit for law firms that covers the terms, the pages, the outside profiles and what you can actually measure. Written by Bryan Driscoll and Everett Sizemore Published: October 13, 2026 Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is becoming an important part of legal marketing as AI-assisted search changes how prospective clients discover and evaluate lawyers. This guide explains the fundamentals of GEO, how it relates to SEO and other AI search concepts, practical strategies firms can apply, and the metrics that can help measure visibility in AI-generated results. GEO for law firms focuses on how AI search tools describe a firm rather than on where its pages rank. Ahrefs defines the goal as getting noticed and accurately represented in AI-generated answers , even when nobody clicks through. That representation rests on the public record, which is the core of what AI visibility means for a law firm . AI tools are already describing your firm from whatever public information exists. Summary prepared by AI search is already shaping how prospective clients find law firms, making visibility and accuracy urgent priorities for firm leaders and legal marketers. GEO builds on SEO: clarify lawyer and firm details, strengthen priority pages, update credible third-party profiles and maintain a crawlable website. A seven-step audit helps identify gaps quickly, while Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools and GA4 track citations, visibility, referrals and conversions. Read the full guide to turn scattered online information into a consistent public record that supports client discovery. How Do GEO, AEO and AIO Differ? If you ask the practitioners themselves, many will say these are just three different ways to refer to the same practice. However, certain subtle differences have begun to emerge, which we will cover here. GEO, or Generative Engine Optimization is more often used to describe optimizations made to increase the likelihood that your brand (in this case a lawyer or legal practice) gets cited, mentioned or recommended in responses generated by AI chatbots and agents like ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, Claude (chat and co-work) and Microsoft's Co-Pilot. We will cover the differences between citations, mentions and recommendations later. AEO, or Answer Engine Optimization , generally narrows optimizations made to show up in answers to search queries, such as Google's AI Overviews, or AI-based search engines like Perplexity. It is the least used of the three terms discussed here. AIO, or AI Optimization , is broader and often used interchangeably with GEO, AEO, or AI search optimization in general. Many practitioners believe it is the best way to describe the practice. However, if you ask ten practitioners about these three acronyms, you are likely to get ten different answers. The terms overlap and are still settling. Search Engine Land's 2025 research found GEO recognized by 84% of the marketers it surveyed and AIO by fewer than half . Marketers keep stacking newer labels drawn from large language models (LLMs), including LLM optimization for lawyers, but none of them changes the underlying work. Still others maintain that it is all just SEO, and Google seems to be in that camp. For the purpose of this guide, let us focus on GEO, and more specifically GEO for law firms. How do you get generative engines, or generative search engines, to cite your content, or recommend your attorneys or law firm? Does GEO Replace SEO? GEO does not replace SEO. Crawlability, indexing, relevance, site structure and useful content are the fundamentals GEO for law firms builds on, while it extends the focus to AI-generated answers, citations, entity clarity and the firm's broader digital presence. The change shows up in the traffic, because AI answers now absorb much of the informational search traffic legal content used to earn . Is SEO Dead Now With AI? SEO is not dead. Google's documentation states that there are no additional requirements for appearing in AI Overviews or AI Mode and that everything it recommends is standard SEO. Much of what gets sold as AI SEO for law firms is that same work under a newer name. Is GEO Replacing SEO? GEO is not replacing SEO. Ahrefs points out that AI answers still pull from traditional search indexes, so the SEO work you already do supports AI visibility. Do that SEO work first and then add the GEO steps on top of it. Waiting on AI optimization for law firms buys nothing, because AI answers keep coming either way. How to Optimize a Law Firm for GEO GEO for law firms runs as a seven-step audit, starting with what AI tools say about your firm now and working back to the pages they read. 1. Establish Your Baseline Now that client discovery is moving into AI search tools , enter several high-value searches a prospective client would run in the major tools. Record whether your firm appears and whether your lawyers appear individually, since GEO for lawyers is a separate question. Then note the competitors, the cited sources and whether the description gets your firm right. Write the results down so the next run has something to measure against. The same manual routine, documented by Ahrefs, checks the description against the facts. Accuracy matters more for a law firm, because a wrong practice area or jurisdiction sends you the wrong client or sends the right client elsewhere. 2. Audit Your Priority Pages Begin with attorney bios, core practice area pages, location pages, about and firm pages plus your highest-value informational content, because that is where clients and AI tools are most likely to look. For each page, check indexing, topic clarity, the location and jurisdiction it covers, freshness, the internal links pointing to it and whether it is readable by people and by machines. Google's guidance covers the mechanics, from checking indexing in Search Console to using internal links as a crawler's path. 3. Make Firm and Lawyer Information Explicit Check that names, firm affiliation, titles, locations, practice areas, credentials and bio information read the same way everywhere they appear, so the relationship between a lawyer, the firm, the location and the expertise is easy to follow. Semrush explains that inconsistent naming across a brand's properties makes the entity harder to recognize and that uniform identifiers are the fix. That consistency is what entity SEO for lawyers means in practice. It is work a firm can finish, because those are specific facts, down to bar admissions and office locations. 4. Check Topic Coverage Look at whether your site covers the questions and related topics prospective clients bring. Before answering, AI Overviews and AI Mode may run extra searches on surrounding subtopics and pull from more than one data source, which Google calls query fan-out. Semantic SEO for lawyers asks you to cover a client's whole problem, which gives those searches more to find. Build out from the plain language questions behind each practice area . 5. Keep Important Content Clear, Current and Verifiable Give the important pages direct answers, headings that describe what follows, accurate sourcing, the jurisdiction and date behind the answer, plus current legal information. Google's people-first content documentation treats trust as the most important of the four qualities it names, ahead of experience, expertise and authoritativeness, and warns against cosmetic date changes on content nobody updated . For the formatting itself, work through how to make legal content easier for AI search to read . 6. Audit Credible Third-Party Sources Review the authoritative outside profiles and publications that describe your firm and its lawyers. Check the firm name, lawyer information, practice areas, locations, professional recognition and anything outdated, inaccurate or conflicting. Generative engines often cite sources your firm has little or no control over. Those sources can confirm or contradict what you publish about yourself . If an AI-generated answer omits a practice area your firm handles, check the sources it cites to see where the incomplete information may be coming from. Correct the source where possible. If the publisher does not respond, strengthen the information available elsewhere by updating your website, legal directory profiles and other credible third-party sources, so your firm’s capabilities are consistently represented. 7. Check the Technical Foundation Google says no new files, AI-specific text files or extra markup are needed to appear in its AI features. Rather than publishing separate markdown versions of your content or putting significant effort into llms.txt files, focus on making your site crawlable, indexable and easy for search and AI systems to access. Pay particular attention to how important pages appear when JavaScript is disabled, since some AI crawlers and agents may not render JavaScript when accessing web pages. Make sure internal links connect priority pages, important content is present in the underlying HTML and any structured data you use is a supported type that matches what visitors can see. There is no special GEO schema, and no markup guarantees an AI citation. Run a GEO Check Use the quick version when you do not have time for the full audit. What it turns up tells you which step your firm needs first. Pick three high-value searches. Check them across two or three AI search tools. Record which firms and sources appear. Review five priority URLs. Compare firm and attorney information across your own pages and outside sources. Check the AI Performance report in Bing Webmaster Tools if available. Identify the three biggest gaps and prioritize them. How to Measure GEO Measuring the success of your law firm’s GEO efforts comes down to AI citations, cited URLs, grounding queries, mentions of your firm and lawyers, AI referral traffic, conversions and changes in visibility over time. Google Search Console now includes a Generative AI performance report , which shows how your site performs in Google Search’s generative AI features. It can be used to track impressions over time, identify which pages appear most often and see where those impressions originate by device or country. Bing Webmaster Tools provides additional detail through its AI Performance report , which tracks citation activity across Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI-generated experiences and select partner integrations. It includes total citations, cited pages, visibility trends and grounding queries, or the phrases used to retrieve content that was cited in AI-generated answers. Bing has also added features such as Topics, Intents and Citation Share to provide more context around where and why content appears. GA4 can then help measure traffic arriving from AI platforms and what those visitors do after reaching your site through its native AI Assistant channel . Use referral traffic and conversion data alongside Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools to evaluate whether greater AI visibility is translating into meaningful website activity. Make AI Visibility a Coordinated Effort Your practice area pages, your attorney bios and the outside profiles carrying your name are the material an AI answer about your firm draws on, and GEO for law firms works best when all three agree. That public record exists whether or not you tend it, so the work is keeping it consistent. You can strengthen that record with the Best Lawyers Digital Marketing Platform , across lawyer and firm profiles, content, backlinks and trusted third-party sources, as part of a broader public footprint. text: To get your law firm cited by ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews, publish answer-first, self-contained content with schema markup, build topical depth across practice areas, optimize E-E-A-T signals through attorney bylines and credentials, and structure guides with direct answers, FAQ sections, and inline citations to authoritative sources. To get your law firm cited by ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews, publish definitive, answer-first content on high-authority domains, mark it with schema vocabulary answer engines can parse, and build a citation graph of practitioner profiles, case outcomes, and topical depth that signals expertise. Research by SparkToro found that only 11% of websites cited by both engines overlap, which means law firms need tailored strategies for each platform—ChatGPT prioritizes semantic depth and recent web retrieval, while Google AI Overviews weight E-E-A-T signals and structured data. AI search visibility strategies related guide related guide related guide related guide seo for med spas why invisible in ai search related guide related guide AI-driven search now shapes how potential clients discover legal counsel. Google's AI Overviews appear in over 16% of queries , while ChatGPT handles tens of millions of daily sessions in which users ask for attorney recommendations, case guidance, and jurisdiction-specific advice. When your firm appears as a cited source in those answers, you earn visibility that bypasses traditional SERP competition and establishes authority before the prospect even clicks. This guide provides the precise steps to optimize your site, content, and technical infrastructure so answer engines quote you—not your competitors. Why answer engines matter for law firm marketing Traditional SEO for lawyers optimizes for ten blue links; generative engine optimization (GEO) optimizes for zero clicks—or for the right click after an AI summary establishes trust. When a potential client asks ChatGPT "Who is the best estate planning attorney in Austin?" or Google surfaces an AI Overview for "How much does a personal injury lawyer charge?", the firms named in that response capture attention at the moment of highest intent. One analysis by Authoritas reported that brands cited in Google AI Overviews earned approximately 120% more organic clicks per impression than uncited competitors, suggesting that AI visibility functions as a trust signal even when users continue to organic results. Meanwhile, research from Forward Push indicated that ChatGPT-referred traffic converted at 15.9% and Perplexity at 10.5%—higher than many paid channels—though conversion rates vary widely by practice area, geography, and content quality. The common thread: answer engines surface firms that demonstrate topical authority, practitioner credentials, and content designed to be quoted. How Google AI Overviews decide which law firms to cite Google AI Overviews synthesize Search Generative Experience (SGE) prototypes with the company's existing ranking and quality systems. According to Google's documentation , AI Overviews pull from "high-quality sources" already indexed by Google Search, applying E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness) criteria to filter candidates. A Moz study of 12,000 AI Overview citations found that 96% of cited pages met baseline E-E-A-T thresholds—verified authorship, topical depth, and external validation. Structured data also matters: 73% of cited pages used schema markup, compared to 42% across the broader web. For law firms, this means Google weighs your attorney bios, published case results, bar admissions, peer recognition, and the clarity of your content architecture when deciding whether to quote you. Citations cluster around three content types: Definitive guides that answer a single question comprehensively (e.g., "What are grounds for divorce in California?"). Practitioner profiles with structured credentials, jurisdictions, and practice-area taxonomy. Comparison or procedural content that walks users through a decision or process (e.g., "Steps to file a trademark application"). Google does not cite thin service pages, generic "About" copy, or content that merely repackages other sources without original analysis or case-specific insight. How ChatGPT and Perplexity select legal sources ChatGPT combines parametric knowledge—facts learned during pre-training—with real-time web retrieval powered by Bing (for ChatGPT Plus and Enterprise) or plugins. According to OpenAI's research blog , the model prioritizes sources that match semantic intent, exhibit consistent citation from authoritative domains, and provide self-contained, quotable passages. Unlike Google, ChatGPT does not apply traditional PageRank or backlink analysis. Instead, it evaluates: Semantic coherence: Does the page directly answer the user's query in the first 200 words? Source reputation: Has the domain been cited frequently in legal contexts across the model's training data? Recency signals: For time-sensitive queries (statute changes, recent precedents), the model weights newer publication dates. Perplexity operates similarly but surfaces inline citations with URLs, making it easier to trace which domains the engine trusts. An analysis by SparkToro showed that Perplexity cited .edu and .gov domains 2.8× more often than commercial sites, but law firms with attorney-authored, schema-tagged case guides appeared at rates comparable to university legal clinics. The upshot: both engines reward clarity, depth, and verifiable authorship. A 400-word blog post titled "Why You Need a Lawyer" will never be cited; a 2,000-word guide on "How Texas Courts Calculate Child Support: Formula, Exceptions, and Modification Procedures" authored by a named family-law partner stands a strong chance. Seven steps to make your law firm AI-citable 1. Publish answer-first, self-contained content Answer engines extract passages that function as standalone responses. Structure every guide with a direct, definitive answer in the opening paragraph , followed by supporting detail, examples, and procedural steps. Before (non-citable): "Child support in Texas is a complex area of family law. Many factors come into play, and it's important to consult an attorney." After (citable): "Texas family courts calculate child support using a percentage-of-income model defined in Texas Family Code § 154.125. For one child, the noncustodial parent typically pays 20% of net resources; for two children, 25%; scaling to 40% for five or more. Courts may deviate from the guideline when a parent's net resources exceed $9,200 per month or when the child has special needs." The second version can be quoted verbatim by an AI engine because it answers "How does Texas calculate child support?" in a complete, fact-dense paragraph. 2. Mark attorney profiles with LegalService and Attorney schema Structured data helps answer engines parse credentials, practice areas, and jurisdictions. Implement schema.org/LegalService on practice-area pages and schema.org/Attorney (or schema.org/Person with jobTitle and memberOf properties) on attorney bios. Minimal Attorney schema example: { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "Attorney", "name": "Jane Doe", "url": "https://example.com/attorneys/jane-doe", "jobTitle": "Partner, Family Law", "alumniOf": { "@type": "EducationalOrganization", "name": "University of Texas School of Law" }, "memberOf": { "@type": "Organization", "name": "State Bar of Texas" }, "areaServed": "Austin, TX", "knowsAbout": ["Child Custody", "Divorce", "Child Support"] } Google uses this markup to surface attorney names and credentials in AI Overviews when users ask "Who is a family law attorney in Austin?" ChatGPT does not parse JSON-LD directly, but schema-tagged pages rank higher in Bing (ChatGPT's web-retrieval backend), increasing the likelihood of inclusion in real-time results. 3. Build topical depth with pillar-and-cluster architecture Answer engines favor domains that demonstrate comprehensive coverage of a subject. For each core practice area, publish: One pillar page (2,500–4,000 words) that surveys the entire topic (e.g., "Texas Family Law: A Complete Guide"). 8–12 cluster articles (1,200–2,000 words each) that dive into subtopics (e.g., "How to Modify a Child Custody Order in Texas," "Spousal Maintenance Eligibility Under Texas Law"). Internal links from clusters back to the pillar and between related clusters. This architecture signals to retrieval models that your firm has deep, interconnected expertise. When ChatGPT or Perplexity scans your domain, the density of interlinked, on-topic content increases the probability that at least one page will match a given query. 4. Add FAQ sections to every guide Both Google and ChatGPT surface FAQ content at high rates. Include a "## Frequently Asked Questions" section near the end of each guide, with each question as an H3 heading followed by a 2–4 sentence answer. Example: ### Can I modify child support if I lose my job? Yes. Texas courts allow modification of child support when either parent experiences a material and substantial change in circumstances, including involuntary job loss. You must file a petition and demonstrate the change has lasted or will last at least three months. This format mirrors how users phrase voice and text queries, and the question-answer structure is trivial for language models to extract and quote. 5. Cite authoritative sources inline AI engines trust pages that cite statutes, case law, bar associations, and government resources. Link to: Statutes: Texas Family Code, state legislative sites. Case law: Published opinions (use Google Scholar, Justia, or court databases). Bar associations: State bar ethics opinions, CLE materials. Government agencies: IRS guidance, Social Security Administration rules for family-law implications. Inline citations improve E-E-A-T scores for Google and provide retrieval anchors for ChatGPT. Use descriptive anchor text: [Texas Family Code § 154.125](https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/FA/htm/FA.154.htm) . 6. Optimize for mobile and page speed Google AI Overviews integrate Core Web Vitals into citation selection. A study by HTTP Archive found that pages with Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) under 2.5 seconds were cited 1.9× more often than slower pages, even when content quality was comparable. Run your site through PageSpeed Insights and address: Image compression (use WebP or AVIF). Lazy-loading for below-the-fold content. Minified CSS and JavaScript. A content delivery network (CDN) for static assets. Fast, mobile-friendly pages also improve user experience for the clicks you do earn from AI Overviews and ChatGPT referrals. 7. Publish practitioner bylines and bios Every article should carry a visible byline linking to a full attorney bio. ChatGPT's training data associates authorship with credibility, and Google's E-E-A-T guidelines explicitly call for author transparency . Include: Full name and title. Bar admissions and license numbers (where ethically permissible). Education and honors. Years of practice and case highlights. Professional affiliations (e.g., "Member, American Bar Association Family Law Section"). A robust bio page not only supports the articles it backs but can itself be cited when users ask "Who is a qualified estate planning attorney in [city]?" Common citation-blocking mistakes law firms make Thin service pages with no unique insight A page titled "Personal Injury Lawyer | [City]" that contains 200 words of generic copy ("We fight for your rights") will never be cited. Answer engines need substantive, original analysis—case examples, step-by-step procedures, jurisdiction-specific rules, or data summaries. Fix: Expand service pages into mini-guides. For instance, convert "Personal Injury Lawyer" into "What to Do After a Car Accident in Texas: Evidence, Deadlines, and Compensation," then detail the 72-hour police-report window, comparative negligence rules, and typical settlement timelines. Duplicate or template-driven content Many legal marketing platforms auto-generate practice pages from templates, resulting in near-identical copy across dozens of firms. AI engines detect and deprioritize duplicate content because it offers no new information. Fix: Write every page from scratch, incorporating your firm's case outcomes, local court procedures, and attorney perspectives. If you must use templates, rewrite at least 70% of the body and add unique sections (e.g., "How [Your Firm] Approaches [Issue]" or "Recent [Practice Area] Outcomes We've Achieved"). Missing or generic author bylines Pages without named authors score poorly on E-E-A-T. Bylines like "Admin" or "Marketing Team" fail to establish practitioner authority. Fix: Attribute every article to a licensed attorney. If associates or paralegals draft content, have a partner review, approve, and co-author. Display the attorney's headshot, credentials, and a link to their full bio at the top or bottom of the article. No schema markup Over 73% of pages cited in Google AI Overviews use structured data, yet most law firm sites deploy only basic Organization or LocalBusiness schema. Without Attorney , LegalService , or FAQPage markup, engines cannot efficiently parse your credentials or content. Fix: Implement JSON-LD schema on every attorney bio and practice page. Use Google's Rich Results Test to validate. For WordPress sites, plugins like Schema Pro or Yoast SEO Premium simplify deployment. Ignoring real-time web retrieval in ChatGPT Plus ChatGPT's free tier relies on parametric knowledge with a training cutoff that shifts periodically. ChatGPT Plus and Enterprise users, however, can invoke Bing-powered web search, which retrieves and cites live URLs. If your site has thin crawl depth, slow load times, or robots.txt blocks, you may be invisible to this retrieval layer. Fix: Ensure your site is fully crawlable (check robots.txt and XML sitemaps), submit your sitemap to Bing Webmaster Tools, and verify that key pages load in under 3 seconds. Monitor Bing organic traffic as a proxy for ChatGPT retrieval eligibility. Measuring your AI citation footprint Unlike traditional SEO, where rank tracking and click data are standard, AI citation measurement is still nascent. Use these methods to gauge progress: Manual prompt testing: Query ChatGPT, Google (with AI Overviews enabled in your region), and Perplexity with phrases your clients would use (e.g., "best estate planning attorney in [city]," "how to file for divorce in [state]"). Document which firms are cited and whether yours appears. Referral traffic segmentation: In Google Analytics, create a segment for chatgpt.com , perplexity.ai , and bing.com (ChatGPT's retrieval engine) referrals. Track sessions, bounce rate, and goal completions to assess conversion quality. Brand-mention monitoring: Tools like Brand24, Mention, or Google Alerts can surface when your firm's name appears in AI-generated content shared online (e.g., Reddit threads where users paste ChatGPT recommendations). Bing Webmaster Tools: Monitor impressions and clicks from Bing, which correlates with ChatGPT's web-search backend. Rising Bing visibility often precedes ChatGPT citations. Competitor citation audits: Reverse-engineer competitors' cited pages. Identify the schema they use, content length, and topical angles, then publish deeper, better-sourced alternatives. Track these metrics monthly. Meaningful citation gains typically require 90–180 days of consistent publishing, schema deployment, and link-building to authoritative legal resources. Integrating AI citation strategy into your broader marketing AI visibility complements—but does not replace—traditional law firm marketing channels. Consider this integrated workflow: Content calendar: Publish one pillar guide per quarter and two cluster articles per month, each optimized for both AI citation and organic search. Technical SEO: Audit schema quarterly, monitor Core Web Vitals, and ensure every new attorney bio is marked up within 48 hours of hire. Link building: Earn backlinks from state bar associations, legal directories (Avvo, Justia, FindLaw), and local news outlets. These signals boost both traditional and AI-driven rankings. Paid amplification: Share definitive guides on LinkedIn, sponsor CLE webinars, and run Google Ads to guides (not just service pages) to build initial traffic and backlink velocity. Client education: When AI Overviews or ChatGPT cite your firm, capture screenshots and feature them in newsletters, social proof sections, and pitch decks. Prospective clients value third-party validation, even from algorithms. By weaving AI optimization into existing SEO, content, and PR efforts, you maximize the return on each published asset. Frequently asked questions How long does it take for a law firm to appear in ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews? Most firms see initial citations within 90–180 days of publishing authoritative, schema-tagged content, provided the site already has baseline domain authority and crawl efficiency. Google AI Overviews draw from the existing search index, so pages that rank on page one organically are more likely to be cited quickly. ChatGPT's parametric knowledge updates periodically with new training runs, but its web-retrieval mode can surface recently published pages within days if they rank well in Bing. Consistent publishing, internal linking, and external validation (backlinks from .edu or bar associations) accelerate the timeline. Do I need separate content for ChatGPT versus Google AI Overviews? Not entirely, but emphasis differs. Google AI Overviews prioritize E-E-A-T signals—verified authorship, schema markup, Core Web Vitals—and favor pages already ranking in the top ten. ChatGPT values semantic density and self-contained answers; it is less sensitive to backlink profiles but rewards clear, quotable passages and topical depth. A single piece of content optimized with answer-first structure, attorney bylines, and LegalService schema will perform well in both engines. The main divergence: Google weights local signals (NAP consistency, Google Business Profile) more heavily, while ChatGPT gives equal weight to national or jurisdiction-agnostic content. Can law firms pay to be cited in AI Overviews or ChatGPT? No. Neither Google nor OpenAI offers paid placement within AI-generated answers. Google AI Overviews cite organically indexed pages based on relevance and quality, and any attempt to manipulate citations violates Google's spam policies . ChatGPT's web retrieval pulls from Bing's index, which similarly prohibits paid inclusion in organic results. Law firms can invest in content creation, technical SEO, and link building to improve citation odds, but there is no direct payment mechanism for AI visibility. What practice areas get cited most often by answer engines? Family law, estate planning, immigration, and consumer-facing criminal defense (DUI, expungement) see the highest AI citation rates, likely because these areas generate high search volume with clear, procedural questions ("How do I file for custody?" "What is an I-130 visa?"). Complex commercial litigation, M&A, and securities law appear less frequently because queries are more bespoke and users typically seek direct consultation rather than general guidance. However, publishing thought-leadership content on emerging legal issues—data privacy, cryptocurrency regulation, ESG compliance—can earn citations in niche queries where few competitors have published deeply. Should my law firm remove thin content to improve AI citation chances? Yes, if that content dilutes your site's perceived topical authority. A site with 200 shallow service pages and ten substantive guides signals inconsistency to both Google and retrieval models. Conduct a content audit: for any page under 500 words with no unique insight, either expand it into a comprehensive guide (1,500+ words, schema, FAQ), consolidate it with related pages, or de-index it with a noindex tag. Pruning thin content can improve crawl efficiency, concentrate link equity on your best pages, and raise average content quality—all factors that increase AI citation probability. Final implementation checklist Before you expect consistent AI citations, verify that your site meets these baseline requirements: Every attorney bio includes LegalService or Attorney schema with practice areas, jurisdictions, and credentials. At least one pillar guide per core practice area, each 2,500+ words with answer-first structure and inline statutory or case-law citations. FAQ sections on every guide, with H3 questions and 2–4 sentence answers. Named attorney bylines on all articles, linking to full bios. Mobile-friendly design with LCP under 2.5 seconds and CLS under 0.1. XML sitemap submitted to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. No robots.txt blocks on key content directories. Backlinks from at least three authoritative legal sources (state bar, .edu legal clinic, respected legal publication). Check this list quarterly and update as search engines and AI platforms evolve their citation criteria. The firms that appear most consistently in AI Overviews and ChatGPT results treat content as a core service offering—not an afterthought—and invest in practitioner-authored, schema-rich, citation-grade publishing at the same level they invest in case preparation.
